passage:
Warden's note, Boys' Hostel B, 20 July
Rahil, second year, came to me asking if he could skip the mess and cook instant noodles in his room to "save money". He has also been walking forty minutes to college instead of taking the bus, for the same reason.
Last week, though, his internship bonus came through, and within days he had bought new headphones and a gaming chair, and treated the whole floor to dinner. When I asked, he said, "That was bonus money, ma'am. The bus fare comes from my real money."
He honestly doesn't see it as one pot. I didn't lecture. I asked him to write every rupee he has, from anywhere, on one sheet. His classmate Deepika, who keeps a simple notebook budget, offered to sit with him. They will meet on Sunday. I'll check in next week.
Farida

qa.q: What did Rahil buy after the internship bonus came through?
qa.a: He bought new headphones and a gaming chair, and treated the whole floor to dinner.

qa.q: Why does walking forty minutes feel sensible to Rahil while the gaming chair doesn't feel wasteful?
qa.a: Rahil feels relaxed about spending the bonus because in his mind it is a separate extra pot, while he feels protective of his "real money" and guards the bus fare tightly.

qa.q: What does Farida's one-sheet idea help Rahil see?
qa.a: Writing every rupee on one sheet shows all his money as one pot, so he can see the bonus could have covered a lot of bus rides and mess meals.

qa.q: How might Deepika see Rahil's habits when they sit together?
qa.a: Deepika may find it surprising that someone skipping the bus to save money just spent so much on a chair, and will probably help Rahil see it as one budget.

grounding: It shows a male student spending a bonus freely while pinching on bus fare and meals, because separate mental pots hide his whole picture.

passage:
Wednesday, 9 pm
Had dry bread and tea for dinner again to save forty rupees on the mess extra. I've been proud of this streak. I also skipped photocopying the notes and took photos instead, to save ten.
Then I opened my bank app to check something and saw it: the tax refund from my summer job came in three weeks ago, and I've spent almost all of it. New sneakers. A concert ticket. Snacks for everyone at Tanuja's birthday. I barely remember deciding any of it. It just felt like bonus money, not "mine".
Nikita didi called and I told her. She laughed and said, "Little brother, you're guarding coins and throwing notes." She's right. It's all one wallet.
Tomorrow: one list of everything, refund included.
Aniket

qa.q: What came into Aniket's account three weeks ago?
qa.a: The tax refund from the summer job came in three weeks ago.

qa.q: Why did the refund not feel like Aniket's own money?
qa.a: The refund felt like bonus money, so Aniket spent it carelessly without guilt, while saving forty rupees on dinner made him feel proud of his careful effort.

qa.q: Is Aniket's plan for tomorrow a good start?
qa.a: Yes; putting everything, refund included, on one list lets Aniket see the whole picture and notice the snacks and sneakers cost far more than the savings on meals.

qa.q: What does Nikita didi's line about coins and notes show about how she sees it?
qa.a: She sees the mismatch clearly and finds it a bit funny, but cares enough to point out that all the money comes from one wallet.

grounding: It shows a young man spending a tax refund carelessly while pinching on small daily costs, because he keeps the money in separate mental accounts.

passage: In the small town of Malegaon, Asif, twenty, counted every coin of his daily money. He walked three kilometres to college to save the ten-rupee shared auto, and he told Karthik, his friend from the repair shop where they both worked evenings, that chai at the stall was a luxury. Then the shop owner gave them each an Eid bonus of four thousand rupees. Asif spent his in a week: a big speaker, biryani for six friends, and a day trip to the dam on hired bikes. "Bonus money," he said. "It's extra." In March the exam form fee came due. Asif stood at the college window eight hundred rupees short and borrowed from Karthik, who had quietly kept his bonus aside.

qa.q: How far did Asif walk to college to save the auto fare?
qa.a: He walked three kilometres to save the ten-rupee shared auto.

qa.q: Why did spending the bonus in a week feel fine to Asif?
qa.a: He thought of it as "extra", separate from the daily money he guarded, so it didn't feel like part of his real budget.

qa.q: What could Asif try the next time a bonus arrives?
qa.a: He could look at all his money together, including coming costs like the exam fee, before deciding what the bonus is for.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel lending Asif money for the exam form?
qa.a: Karthik may be glad to help a friend but also a little surprised, having watched Asif fuss over ten-rupee autos and then spend a whole bonus in a week.

grounding: A young man pinches coins on daily costs but spends a bonus freely, and the separate mental pots leave him short when a fee comes due.

passage: In Lyon, Bao kept a tiny notebook of daily costs. He refused the coffee after lectures, carried his lunch in a jar and walked forty minutes to avoid buying a tram ticket. "Every cent counts," he told Ines. Then in June a tax refund of six hundred euros landed, from his part-time job at a bookshop. That wasn't in the notebook. By the end of the month it had become a weekend in Barcelona, a leather jacket and new headphones. "It's refund money," he said when Ines raised an eyebrow. "Free money." In August the rent went up, and the notebook showed Bao three hundred euros short. He stared at the neat list of saved coffees and felt foolish.

qa.q: How much was Bao's tax refund?
qa.a: A tax refund of six hundred euros.

qa.q: Why did Bao call the refund "free money"?
qa.a: It wasn't part of the notebook he tracked so carefully, so it felt separate from his real budget and easy to spend.

qa.q: What turning point shows Bao the problem, and what could he change?
qa.a: Finding himself short when the rent went up; he could put every euro, refunds included, into the same notebook so he sees the whole picture.

qa.q: What might Ines have been thinking on raising an eyebrow?
qa.a: Ines probably found it odd that someone who walked forty minutes to save a tram ticket would spend six hundred euros in a month.

grounding: A student saves small daily amounts but spends a tax refund carelessly, because keeping it in a separate mental account hides his whole situation.

passage:
Supervisor's note, internship programme, 30 June.
Ujjwal, one of our summer interns, puzzles me. He walks two kilometres from the station every morning in the heat to save the auto fare, and he refuses the canteen tea because it costs ten rupees. Yet last week, when the joining bonus arrived, he bought an expensive smartwatch the same afternoon. Vikas, the other intern, mentioned that Ujjwal is short for the hostel deposit due next week. When I asked Ujjwal about it gently, he said, "The bonus was extra. It didn't feel like my real money." He saw the problem as soon as he said it out loud. I didn't lecture. I suggested he list everything coming in and going out this month on one page, and offered him time with our finance officer if he wanted help.

qa.q: How far does Ujjwal walk from the station every morning?
qa.a: He walks two kilometres.

qa.q: Why did the bonus feel fine to spend on a smartwatch?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt happy and relaxed about the bonus as extra, not 'real money', so spending it seemed harmless, while daily costs felt serious enough to pinch.

qa.q: What did the supervisor suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Listing everything coming in and going out on one page, with time offered with the finance officer, so Ujjwal sees the whole picture instead of separate pots.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel about knowing Ujjwal is short for the deposit?
qa.a: Vikas might feel worried for Ujjwal and a little awkward about mentioning it.

grounding: Shows a student pinching on daily costs while spending a bonus at once, because separate mental pots hide the whole picture.

passage:
Wednesday
The college refunded my extra exam fee today: 6,000 rupees! It felt like a gift from the sky, so I booked the Goa trip with Nilesh and the others right away. No second thought.
This evening at the mess I skipped the extra paneer because it's twenty rupees. I've been skipping it all month. I also walked to the market instead of taking the bus, to save fifteen.
Nilesh noticed and laughed. "You'll spend six thousand in a minute and fight over twenty?" I told him the refund was a separate thing. Bonus money. Then he asked what my rent is next month, and whether I have it. I said... not yet.
I think my brain keeps different piggy banks and never adds them up. Tomorrow I'll sit down with Papa on the phone and look at all of it together.
Jeevan

qa.q: How much did the college refund Jeevan?
qa.a: 6,000 rupees.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan book the trip without a second thought?
qa.a: Jeevan felt thrilled and carefree, treating the refund as a gift from the sky, a separate pot from the everyday money being pinched.

qa.q: What is Jeevan planning, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Looking at all the money together with Papa on the phone, so rent, the trip and daily costs are seen as one picture.

qa.q: How does Nilesh see Jeevan's spending?
qa.a: Nilesh finds it funny and odd that Jeevan spends six thousand in a minute but fights over twenty.

grounding: Shows a student spending a refund at once while pinching tiny daily costs, missing the whole picture.

passage:
Manoj, a second-year student in Dharwad, walked twenty minutes each way to college to save the auto fare. He argued with the canteen boy over two rupees for extra chutney and skipped tea most days.

Then his scholarship refund came through, a lump sum he hadn't expected. That same evening he bought a fancy watch at the market, took his friend Chetan out for a big dinner, and ordered new speakers.

"You walked in the heat all month to save ten rupees," Chetan said, "and now this?"

"That was my daily money," Manoj said. "This is extra."

At the end of the month, his phone bill came. He looked at his almost empty account and felt a jolt of panic. The watch ticked on his wrist.

qa.q: What did Manoj buy at the market the evening the refund came?
qa.a: He bought a fancy watch.

qa.q: Why did spending the refund freely feel reasonable to Manoj?
qa.a: He felt excited and carefree because the refund seemed like "extra" money, separate from the daily money he guarded so tightly.

qa.q: What would you advise Manoj to do the next time a refund arrives?
qa.a: He could look at all his money together before spending and talk it over with a parent or a college finance adviser.

qa.q: How does Chetan see Manoj's spending?
qa.a: Chetan is surprised and a little puzzled that Manoj pinches rupees daily but spends a big sum in one evening.

grounding: A student spends a refund carelessly while pinching on small daily costs, keeping money in separate mental pots.

passage:
In Buenos Aires, Santiago worked weekends at a café while studying engineering. He brought lunch from home every day and refused to buy a coffee on campus, even when he was exhausted.

In December the café gave him a holiday bonus. Within a week, he'd spent it on concert tickets, a new jacket, and a weekend trip with friends.

His flatmate Soo-ah watched him refuse a coffee again in January. "You spent your whole bonus in a week, but you won't buy a coffee?"

"The bonus was fun money," Santiago said. "Coffee comes out of my real money."

"It's all your money," Soo-ah said.

Santiago opened his banking app and looked at the total. It was lower than he'd thought, and he felt a little sick.

qa.q: Where did Santiago work on weekends?
qa.a: He worked weekends at a café.

qa.q: How did Santiago feel when he looked at his total in January?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and a little sick, realising his separate "fun" and "real" money were one smaller pile.

qa.q: What could Santiago try so he sees his whole picture?
qa.a: He could look at all his money in one place each month and, if unsure, ask a trusted adult or a bank adviser about choices.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah see Santiago's split between fun money and real money?
qa.a: Soo-ah finds it confusing and a bit worrying, since to her it's all the same money.

grounding: A student spends a bonus freely while pinching on daily costs, keeping separate mental accounts that hide his real picture.

At the college hostel office, Anand was filling in a form when the clerk handed him his fee refund cheque. "Overpaid last semester," she said.

Anand grinned. That weekend he bought a gaming headset and treated his friends at the dhaba.

On Monday his hostel-mate Afreen found him counting coins in the mess queue. "Aren't you getting dal? You love dal."

"Only rice today. I'm saving."

"Saving for what? You just got a refund."

"That was different," Anand mumbled. "That was a bonus."

Afreen sat down next to him. "Show me what you actually have." Anand opened his bank app. The refund was gone, and his mess balance was low. He felt his face go hot.

qa.q: What did the clerk hand Anand?
qa.a: His fee refund cheque.

qa.q: Why did Anand feel his face go hot when he opened his bank app?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and anxious, seeing that the refund was gone and his real balance was low.

qa.q: What small step did Afreen take, and why was it useful?
qa.a: She asked Anand to show what he actually had, which made him look at his whole picture instead of separate pots.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel watching Anand eat only rice?
qa.a: Afreen seems concerned and a little surprised, since she knows he just got a refund.

grounding: A student spends a refund carelessly while pinching on small daily costs, not seeing his whole financial picture.

passage:
Ritu Api,
Confession time. Remember the eight thousand rupees the university refunded from my hostel deposit? Gone. In a week. A concert ticket, a smartwatch, dinner for five people.
The weird part is how careful I am with small things. I walk forty minutes to save a thirty-rupee auto. I skip the canteen tea because ten rupees adds up. I've been doing that all month and feeling very responsible.
Then tonight I added it up. All my walking and tea-skipping this month saved maybe six hundred rupees. The refund was eight thousand. It's like I have two wallets in my head: real money that I guard, and bonus money that doesn't count.
I'm not asking for money. I just needed to say it out loud. Next time something extra comes in, I'll ask Abbu to sit with me before I touch it.
Wasim

qa.q: How much did the university refund?
qa.a: The university refunded eight thousand rupees from the hostel deposit.

qa.q: Why did Wasim feel responsible while the refund vanished?
qa.a: Wasim felt proud and careful skipping tea and walking, while the refund felt like bonus money that didn't count, so the bigger loss went unnoticed.

qa.q: What does Wasim plan for next time, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Asking Abbu to sit together before touching any extra money, so a trusted adult helps look at the whole picture.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel reading the confession?
qa.a: Ritu might feel amused and a little worried, and glad Wasim noticed the two wallets and is being honest.

grounding: Shows a student who spends a refund carelessly while pinching on small daily costs, as if the money sat in separate accounts.

passage:
Uday, you asked how I learned about money. I'm Raghav, and the lesson cost me a whole bonus.
During my internship, the company gave interns a surprise Diwali bonus of ten thousand rupees. I felt rich. That money wasn't real in my head. It was extra, like a gift. So I bought a leather jacket I wore twice, a gaming chair and a weekend in Goa.
Meanwhile I was obsessed with small costs. I argued with an autowala over ten rupees. I carried lunch from the hostel to avoid a sixty-rupee canteen thali.
In January my laptop died, and I needed twelve thousand. That's when I realised I'd never looked at all my money together. The bonus sat in one box in my head, the stipend in another, the canteen money in a third. If I'd seen it as one pile, I'd have kept the bonus for exactly this.
Now I write everything on one list, once a month. Boring. Works.

qa.q: How much was the surprise bonus?
qa.a: The bonus was ten thousand rupees.

qa.q: Why did Raghav spend the bonus so freely?
qa.a: Raghav felt rich and excited, treating the bonus as extra money like a gift, separate from the stipend.

qa.q: What does Raghav do now, and why does it help?
qa.a: Raghav writes all money on one list once a month, so the whole picture is visible before any spending.

qa.q: How might the autowala have seen the argument over ten rupees?
qa.a: The autowala probably found it petty and tiring, a fuss over ten rupees from someone who had just spent thousands.

grounding: Shows a student who spent a bonus carelessly while pinching on small costs, because separate mental accounts hid the whole picture.

passage:
April. Thomas got his first tax refund, six thousand rupees, from his part-time job. "Free money!" he told Raghav, and ordered new running shoes and a speaker the same night.
May. Thomas started counting every small thing. He refused Raghav's offer of a shared auto to save twenty rupees and walked home in the rain. He bought the cheapest biscuits. He felt very disciplined.
June. His college fee instalment was due, and he was short by four thousand. He stared at his banking app. "I've been so careful," he said.
Raghav scrolled through Thomas's spending with him. "Careful with twenty-rupee autos. Not with the six thousand."
Thomas sat back. He had never counted the refund as his money at all. That evening he wrote every rupee coming in and going out on one sheet, and took it to his father to talk it through.

qa.q: How much was Thomas's tax refund?
qa.a: Thomas's tax refund was six thousand rupees.

qa.q: Why did Thomas feel disciplined in May?
qa.a: Thomas felt proud and careful counting small costs, while the refund had felt like free money that didn't count.

qa.q: What did Thomas do in June, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Thomas wrote all money coming in and going out on one sheet and talked it through with his father, so he could see the whole picture.

qa.q: How does Raghav see Thomas's carefulness?
qa.a: Raghav sees that Thomas was careful with small autos but not with the big refund, and points it out plainly.

grounding: Shows a student who spends a tax refund freely while pinching on small costs, until a shortfall reveals the whole picture.

By April, when the exam form fee was due, I had nothing. I had been guarding coins with one hand and throwing notes with the other. I had to borrow from your father, and it took me until Diwali to return it."
